summary.text: An oceanic climate is found in both hemispheres, mostly between 40 and 60 degrees latitude, and is shaped mainly by the ocean and mid-latitude winds.
Water stores heat in the warm months and gives it back slowly in the cold ones, so seasons are less extreme than farther inland.
Westerly winds carry ocean air onto land, and passing storm systems bring changeable weather and rain through much of the year.

items.prompt: A coastal town and an inland town lie at the same latitude. Why does the coastal town have milder seasons?

options.label: The coast gets more hours of sunshine
Sea breezes blow there only in summer
Salt in the air traps heat at night
Water stores heat and releases it slowly

items.explain: Water has a higher heat capacity than land, so it soaks up energy in the warm months and gives it back gradually in the cold ones.

items.prompt: Oceanic climates get frequent rain, yet thunderstorms there are few. Why?

options.label: The air is too dry for storm clouds
Strong heating and clashing air masses are rare
Coastal mountains block every storm
Cold sea air turns all rain to snow

items.explain: Thunderstorms need strong daytime heating or hot and cold air masses meeting, and both happen infrequently in these regions.

items.prompt: Vienna lies far from any ocean, yet it has a maritime climate. What lets sea air reach it?

options.label: Western Europe's low, open land
Moist air carried up the Danube
The Alps funnelling air eastward
Large warm lakes all around it

items.explain: The lowlands of western Europe help drive marine air masses inland; elsewhere a big mountain range or nearby oceans stop oceanic climates spreading far.

items.prompt: Two towns in an oceanic region sit on opposite sides of a mountain range, one facing the moist sea winds. Which one is drier?

options.label: The one facing the sea winds
Both get the same amount
The one on the sheltered side
Whichever is at lower elevation

items.explain: Rising moist air cools and drops rain on the windward slopes, leaving the far side in a rain shadow with much less precipitation.

items.prompt: Ireland, the UK and Norway lie at high latitudes yet have much milder winters than you'd expect. What is credited for this?

options.label: Volcanic heat beneath the North Sea
Warm winds blowing up from the Sahara
A warm current flowing from the tropics
Long winter daylight near the Arctic

items.explain: The Gulf Stream, a tropical current, is thought to greatly modify northwest Europe's climate, and the North Atlantic Current gives these areas much milder winters for their latitude.

items.prompt: In a typical place with an oceanic climate, how often does it snow?

options.label: Never, the sea keeps it too warm
At least once in most years
It covers the ground for months
Only on the coldest mountain tops

items.explain: Rain is the usual form of precipitation, but most oceanic climate zones see at least one snowfall per year.

paragraphs.heading: Mild all year round
paragraphs.text: An oceanic climate has mild summers, cool to mild winters and only a small change in temperature over the year. It occurs in both hemispheres, mostly between 40 and 60 degrees latitude, with subpolar versions reaching 70 degrees on some coasts. The ocean's heat and the mid-latitude wind patterns shape it most.

paragraphs.heading: The sea as a heat store
paragraphs.text: Water can hold more heat than land. It soaks up solar energy through the warm months and gives it back slowly in the cold ones, so coasts have smaller seasonal swings than inland places at the same latitude. In the mid-latitudes, winds from the west often carry ocean air onto land. Passing storm systems with their fronts keep the weather changing and bring rain through much of the year.

paragraphs.heading: Grey skies and drizzle
paragraphs.text: The polar jet stream flows west to east across the middle latitudes and pushes storms and fronts along. In autumn, winter and early spring, when it is most active, marine weather systems pass often, bringing fog, cloudy skies and light drizzle. Thunderstorms are few, because strong daytime heating and meetings of hot and cold air masses are rare there. Most precipitation falls as rain, though most oceanic zones see at least one snowfall a year.

paragraphs.heading: Europe's mild west
paragraphs.text: The Gulf Stream, a tropical ocean current that runs up the US East Coast and then heads toward Newfoundland, is thought to greatly change northwest Europe's climate. Thanks to the North Atlantic Current, Ireland, the UK and Norway have much milder winters than their latitude would suggest. Low land lets sea air push deep into the continent, so Dresden, Prague and Vienna have maritime climates though they sit far from the coast. Only in Europe does this climate reach so far inland; elsewhere mountains or nearby oceans stop it.

paragraphs.heading: Köppen's limits and a cold cousin
paragraphs.text: In Köppen's scheme, the coldest month averages 0 °C or higher (or −3 °C), which separates oceanic from continental climates. The warmest month stays below 22 °C, so summers are warm but not hot. Further poleward lies the subpolar oceanic climate, Köppen Cfc, with long but fairly mild winters and short, cool summers. Examples include parts of coastal Iceland, the Falkland Islands and the far south of Chile and Argentina, around Punta Arenas and Ushuaia.

paragraphs.heading: Mild is not the same as steady
paragraphs.text: Single years can still bring heat waves, cold spells, droughts and downpours. In the North Atlantic, a pattern called the North Atlantic Oscillation is a major source of this variation: when the gap in pressure between the Azores High and the Icelandic Low changes, it shifts the westerly winds and storm tracks. Mountains matter too. Moist sea air rising over them cools and drops more rain on the windward slopes, while the sheltered leeward side gets less, so rainfall can differ a lot over short distances.
